channel.title: Reasoning on Best of AI
channel.description: Recent content in Reasoning on Best of AI

item.title: Claude Fable 5.1
item.description: Anthropic released Claude Fable 5.1 on September 1, 2026, alongside Mythos 5.1, a restricted-access version of the same underlying model available to vetted cybersecurity and life-sciences organizations that need capabilities the public release keeps guarded. Fable 5.1 keeps the same $10 per million input and $50 per million output token pricing as Fable 5, but cuts prompt-cache reads from $1.00 to $0.25 per million tokens, a change Anthropic says lowers effective cost by around 25 percent for typical workloads and as much as 45 percent for heavily agentic ones that lean on cached context. Anthropic reported 52.6 percent on Terminal-Bench-Science as one of the headline benchmark gains over the original Fable 5.

item.title: GPT-6 Astra
item.description: OpenAI launched GPT-6 Astra on September 3, 2026, its most capable model yet and the first to use what the company calls recurrent depth, a looped reasoning technique that lets the model revisit and refine its read of a problem multiple times rather than reasoning in a single forward pass. Pricing runs $10 per million input tokens, $1 for cached input, $12.50 for cache writes, and $50 per million output tokens, with a 1.05 million token context window and up to 128,000 tokens of output. The approach has drawn scrutiny from outside safety researchers, including groups at Redwood Research, who note that recurrent depth makes the model’s chain of thought harder for outside observers to monitor compared with earlier step-by-step reasoning models.

item.title: Muse Spark 1.3
item.description: Meta shipped Muse Spark 1.3 on September 2, 2026, its biggest coding and agentic jump yet and, according to AI chief Alexandr Wang, a model that closes much of the gap with frontier releases like GPT-5.6. It cuts token usage by 25 percent and tool calls by 20 percent on comparable tasks, and holds the same $1.25 per million input and $4.25 per million output token pricing as its predecessor, plus a contributor tier at a steep discount for developers who let Meta train on their prompts and completions. Access starts through Muse Code and the Meta API, with a “max reasoning” variant still going through safety testing before release, and a rollout to Meta AI, Instagram, and Facebook planned to follow.

item.title: Grok 4.6
item.description: xAI released Grok 4.6 on August 12, 2026, extending Grok 4.5’s coding focus toward longer-running agent sessions and more demanding interactive and visual tasks. The model carries a 500,000-token context window, accepts text and image input, and exposes configurable reasoning effort levels from low to xhigh so developers can trade off latency against depth on a given request. xAI priced it at $2 per million input tokens and $6 per million output tokens for prompts under 200,000 tokens, with rates roughly doubling once a request crosses that threshold.

item.title: Kimi K3
item.description: Kimi K3 is Moonshot AI’s largest release yet, a 2.8 trillion parameter mixture-of-experts model that the company says is the biggest open-weight model shipped by anyone so far. It reads text, images, and video natively, carries a 1 million token context window, and runs in an always-on thinking mode rather than offering a separate fast path. Moonshot priced API access at $3 per million input tokens (dropping to $0.30 on a cache hit) and $15 per million output tokens, undercutting closed frontier models from Western labs by a wide margin. Full weights landed on Hugging Face shortly after the July 16 announcement, using MXFP4 quantization to bring the download to roughly 1.4 TB, small enough for serious self-hosting setups to run without a dedicated cluster.

item.title: Ling-3.0-Flash
item.description: Ling-3.0-Flash is the latest entry in Ant Group’s efficiency-focused Ling line, built by its inclusionAI lab and unveiled July 23, 2026 as a hybrid-reasoning foundation model for production AI agent workloads. It’s a 124 billion parameter mixture-of-experts model that activates only about 5.1 billion parameters per token, natively supports a 256,000 token context window that can scale up to 1 million, and Ant says it matches or beats models two to three times its parameter count on reasoning, instruction following, and long-context benchmarks. A cluster-level hierarchical caching system cuts time-to-first-token on long conversations by 60 to 80 percent. Ant priced the first-party API at $0.075 per million input tokens and $0.22 per million output tokens, among the cheapest rates measured for a model scoring 38 or above on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index, and released the weights on Hugging Face under the MIT license.

item.title: Claude Opus 4.5
item.description: Claude Opus 4.5 is the Opus-tier model Anthropic released on November 24, 2025, and its headline change was price: input tokens dropped to $5 per million and output to $25 per million, a two-thirds cut from Opus 4.1’s $15/$75 rate. It scored 80.9 percent on SWE-bench Verified at launch, ahead of Gemini 3 Pro’s 76.2 percent and GPT-5.1 Codex Max’s 77.9 percent on the same benchmark, and Anthropic added an “effort” parameter that lets developers dial reasoning depth up or down per request. It kept the 200,000 token context window and image input support from earlier Opus releases, and shipped alongside a round of Claude Code updates aimed at longer autonomous coding sessions. Anthropic followed it with Opus 4.6 in February 2026 and Opus 4.7 in April, each holding the same $5/$25 pricing while pushing coding scores further.

item.title: Claude Opus 4.6
item.description: Claude Opus 4.6, released February 5, 2026, expanded the Opus line’s context window to 1 million tokens, up from the 200,000 tokens Opus 4.5 shipped with three months earlier. Anthropic held pricing steady at $5 per million input tokens and $25 per million output tokens and focused the update on coding: the model plans more carefully before writing code, sustains agentic tasks over longer sessions, and catches more of its own mistakes during code review. It’s available across claude.ai, the Claude API, and the major cloud platforms, and it became the base Anthropic built the Sonnet 4.6 release on two weeks later.

item.title: Claude Opus 4.7
item.description: Claude Opus 4.7, released April 16, 2026, is a direct upgrade to Opus 4.6 aimed at the hardest software engineering tasks, the ones where earlier Opus models still stumbled on large, unfamiliar codebases. Pricing held at $5 per million input tokens and $25 per million output tokens, and it kept the 1 million token context window with up to 128,000 tokens of output. It shipped with a new tokenizer that produces up to 35 percent more tokens for the same input text, a tradeoff Anthropic made to improve accuracy on code-heavy prompts. It’s available through claude.ai, the API, Amazon Bedrock, Google Vertex AI, and Microsoft Foundry.

item.title: Claude Opus 5
item.description: Claude Opus 5 is Anthropic’s newest Opus-tier model, released July 24, 2026 at the same $5/$25 per million token pricing as Opus 4.8, half of what the larger Claude Fable 5 model charges for similar intelligence. It ships with a low, medium, and high effort toggle so developers can trade cost against reasoning depth on a per-request basis, plus a faster mode that doubles the price to $10/$50 in exchange for roughly 2.5 times the speed. On SWE-bench Pro it scored 79.2 percent, roughly double the agentic coding score Anthropic reported for the previous Opus generation, and it posted 43.3 percent on Frontier-Bench and 30.2 percent on ARC-AGI-3. It carries the 1 million token context window that has been standard across the Opus line since Opus 4.6, and it’s available on claude.ai, the API, and the major cloud platforms from launch.

item.title: Claude Sonnet 4.6
item.description: Claude Sonnet 4.6 shipped on February 17, 2026 and became the default model in claude.ai and Claude Cowork, Anthropic’s workspace product. It matches Opus 4.6’s 1 million token context window and 128,000 token output limit while pricing in at $3 per million input tokens and $15 per million output tokens, roughly a fifth of Opus 4.6’s rate. On SWE-bench Verified it scored 79.6 percent, within a few points of the Opus model despite the price gap, and it posted 59.1 percent on Terminal-Bench 2.0 and 72.5 percent on OSWorld-Verified, benchmarks that test agentic terminal and computer-use tasks. Anthropic built in extended reasoning chains that can run up to 100 steps, aimed at developers who want Opus-level reliability without paying Opus prices.

item.title: DeepSeek V3.2
item.description: DeepSeek V3.2 is DeepSeek’s update to V3.1, publicly detailed on December 1, 2025 after an experimental preview in September. It introduces DeepSeek Sparse Attention, a fine-grained sparse attention mechanism that cuts training and inference cost while preserving quality on long-context tasks, and the flagship Speciale variant carries roughly 685 billion parameters in a mixture-of-experts layout. The context window sits at 163,840 tokens with up to 64,000 tokens of output, and DeepSeek reports gold-medal-level results on 2025 International Mathematical Olympiad and International Olympiad in Informatics problem sets. API pricing runs around $0.21 per million input tokens and $0.32 per million output tokens, roughly half of what V3.1-Terminus cost, particularly for long-context decoding. Like the rest of the DeepSeek lineup it ships under the MIT license with weights on Hugging Face, and it served as the base DeepSeek built V4-Pro on the following spring.

item.title: Gemini 3 Deep Think
item.description: Gemini 3 Deep Think is Google’s extended-reasoning mode for Gemini 3, built for the hardest math, science, and logic problems where a quick answer isn’t good enough. Rather than responding immediately, it explores multiple solution paths in parallel and checks its own logic before committing to an answer, which comes at the cost of much higher latency than Gemini 3 Pro. It scored 41.0 percent on Humanity’s Last Exam, more than 11 points ahead of GPT-5.1 on the same benchmark at the time. Access is gated behind Google’s AI Ultra subscription, which starts at $99.99 a month and requires the $199.99 tier specifically for Deep Think, so it isn’t reachable through the standard Gemini API the way Google’s other models are.

item.title: Gemini 3.1 Pro
item.description: Gemini 3.1 Pro is Google’s generally available successor to Gemini 3 Pro, released February 19, 2026 with a 1 million token context window and up to 64,000 tokens of output across text, image, video, and audio. Google reports 80.6 percent on SWE-bench Verified, 94.3 percent on GPQA Diamond, and 77.1 percent on ARC-AGI-2, where it placed second behind OpenAI’s GPT-5.5. Pricing held at $2.00 per million input tokens and $12.00 per million output tokens for prompts under 200,000 tokens, doubling to $4.00/$18.00 beyond that threshold, with cached input available at $0.20 per million. It’s available through the Gemini app, Google AI Studio, Vertex AI, and the Gemini API, and it remained Google’s flagship model until Gemini 3.5 Pro’s rollout later in 2026.

item.title: GPT-5 Pro
item.description: GPT-5 Pro is the highest-compute variant of GPT-5, released October 6, 2025 for tasks where accuracy matters more than speed or cost. It shares GPT-5’s 400,000 token context window with up to 272,000 tokens of output, and OpenAI prices it well above the standard model at $15 per million input tokens and $120 per million output tokens. It runs longer internal reasoning chains than default GPT-5, trading latency for higher accuracy on hard math, science, and coding problems, and it’s available through ChatGPT Pro and the API rather than the free or Plus tiers. OpenAI kept the same pattern with Pro variants of each GPT-5.x release that followed.

item.title: GPT-5.1
item.description: GPT-5.1 is OpenAI’s update to GPT-5, released November 13, 2025 with an emphasis on coding and agentic tasks. It carries the same 400,000 token context window as GPT-5, with up to 128,000 tokens of output, and API pricing held at $1.25 per million input tokens and $10 per million output tokens, with cached input priced at $0.125 per million. The model exposes a reasoning-effort setting with none, low, medium, and high options, giving developers more control over how much internal deliberation a request gets than GPT-5’s automatic routing offered. OpenAI positioned it as a refinement rather than a new generation, shipped to close gaps competitors had opened up on coding benchmarks in the months since GPT-5’s August 2025 launch.

item.title: GPT-5.2
item.description: GPT-5.2 arrived December 11, 2025 in three variants: GPT-5.2 Instant for quick responses, GPT-5.2 Thinking for step-by-step reasoning, and GPT-5.2 Pro for the hardest problems. It kept the 400,000 token context window and 128,000 token output limit from the GPT-5.1 generation, and OpenAI priced the standard model at $1.75 per million input tokens and $14 per million output tokens, with a five-level reasoning effort setting from minimal to extra high. By mid-2026 OpenAI was steering users toward the newer GPT-5.6 line, but GPT-5.2 remains available in the API and ChatGPT’s legacy model picker.

item.title: GPT-5.4
item.description: GPT-5.4, released March 5, 2026, was the first general-purpose OpenAI model to ship with native computer-use capability, reaching 75 percent on the OSWorld benchmark for controlling a desktop environment directly. It expanded the context window to roughly 1 million tokens (922,000 input plus 128,000 output), added a five-level reasoning effort control, and introduced a tool-search mechanism that OpenAI says cuts token costs by 47 percent in workflows that call a lot of external tools. Standard API pricing is $2.50 per million input tokens and $15 per million output tokens, with a GPT-5.4 Pro tier at $30/$180 for maximum accuracy. OpenAI followed up on March 17 with GPT-5.4 Mini, priced at $0.75/$4.50 and available to free ChatGPT users, plus a developer-only GPT-5.4 Nano tier.

item.title: GPT-5.5
item.description: GPT-5.5, released April 23, 2026 with API access following the next day, pushed the context window to roughly 1 million tokens and lands meaningfully above GPT-5.4 on long-context recall, multi-step tool use, and code generation in large repositories, though it costs more per token. Standard pricing is $5 per million input tokens and $30 per million output tokens, with GPT-5.5 Pro available at $30/$180 for the hardest problems, and OpenAI offers batch and flex pricing at half the standard rate alongside a 2.5 times priority tier for latency-sensitive use. It topped the ARC-AGI-2 leaderboard at roughly 85 percent, the highest score any model had reached on that benchmark at the time, and OpenAI replaced it with GPT-5.6 less than three months later.

item.title: Grok 4.20
item.description: Grok 4.20 is xAI’s multi-agent model, with a beta launching February 17, 2026 and the dated release following on March 9. Its defining feature is a native four-agent system, internally named Grok, Harper, Benjamin, and Lucas, that reasons in parallel and debates internally before returning a single answer, which xAI says cut hallucinations by 65 percent compared to Grok 4.1. It runs on a roughly 3 trillion parameter mixture-of-experts backbone with a context window up to 2 million tokens, operates in separate reasoning and non-reasoning modes, and keeps the real-time X data integration xAI has used across the Grok line. API pricing is $1.25 per million input tokens, $0.20 for cached input, and $2.50 per million output tokens, well below the $2/$6 xAI charged for Grok 4.5 seven months earlier.

item.title: Mistral Large 4
item.description: Mistral Large 4 replaces Large 3 as Mistral AI’s proprietary flagship, roughly eight months after that model shipped in December 2025. It’s a 190 billion parameter dense model with a 256,000 token context window, priced at $2 per million input tokens and $8 per million output tokens through Mistral’s own La Plateforme as well as Azure AI Foundry and AWS Bedrock. Mistral says the gains over Large 3 are concentrated in coding and multi-step reasoning, an area where the company has been trying to close the gap with GPT-5.6 and Claude Sonnet 5 rather than compete on raw scale.

item.title: AlphaGeometry
item.description: AlphaGeometry is a neuro-symbolic system from Google DeepMind, published in Nature in January 2024, built to solve geometry problems at the level of International Mathematical Olympiad competitors. It pairs a language model trained on synthetically generated geometry proofs with a traditional symbolic deduction engine: the neural half proposes useful auxiliary constructions, such as new points or lines, and the symbolic half runs formal logical deduction to complete the proof. On a benchmark of 30 IMO geometry problems from 2000 to 2022, it solved 25, close to the average gold medalist’s score and far ahead of prior automated theorem provers.

item.title: Claude 3.7 Sonnet
item.description: Claude 3.7 Sonnet, released by Anthropic in February 2025, is the company’s first hybrid reasoning model. A single model can answer normally like a standard chat model or switch into an extended thinking mode where it works through a problem step by step before responding, and developers can control how much thinking budget the model uses through the API. This design let Anthropic ship one model that covers both quick everyday questions and harder math, coding, and logic problems, instead of maintaining separate fast and reasoning-focused models. It kept the same 200,000 token context window and $3/$15 per million token pricing as Claude 3.5 Sonnet, and it launched alongside Claude Code, Anthropic’s command-line coding agent, which used 3.7 Sonnet as its default model.

item.title: Claude Fable 5
item.description: Claude Fable 5 is a public, safety-restricted release of Mythos, an internal Anthropic model class that the company unveiled in April 2026 and initially withheld from general availability because of its advanced cybersecurity capabilities. Anthropic made Fable 5 available to enterprise customers and paid subscribers on June 9, 2026, after adding safeguards that redirect queries in high-risk areas like cybersecurity and biology to Claude Opus 4.8 instead, a mechanism the company says triggers in under 5 percent of sessions. On paper it is the strongest model Anthropic has shipped publicly: 95.0 percent on SWE-bench Verified, 80.3 percent on the harder SWE-bench Pro, and 92.6 percent on GPQA Diamond, with strong results in vision and scientific research tasks as well. It carries a 1 million token context window and is priced at $10 per million input tokens and $50 per million output tokens, double what Anthropic charges for Opus 4.8, reflecting its positioning as a specialty top-tier option rather than a general daily driver.

item.title: Claude Opus 4
item.description: Claude Opus 4 launched on May 22, 2025 as Anthropic’s flagship model, released alongside the smaller Claude Sonnet 4. It was built for sustained, long-horizon agentic work such as multi-hour coding sessions and research tasks that involve using tools repeatedly across a long thread, rather than answering a single prompt. Anthropic reported it leading on SWE-bench Verified at launch, at roughly 72.5 percent, and it can use tools, including web search, during extended thinking and run several tools in parallel. It runs on a 200,000 token context window, reads images as well as text, and is priced at $15 per million input tokens and $75 per million output tokens, the same rate Anthropic had charged for Claude 3 Opus a year earlier.

item.title: Claude Opus 4.1
item.description: Claude Opus 4.1, released in August 2025, is a targeted update to Claude Opus 4 rather than a new generation. Anthropic focused the update on coding and agentic accuracy, and it pushed the SWE-bench Verified score up to roughly 74.5 percent, a meaningful jump on the real-world GitHub issue benchmark that Anthropic uses to track coding ability. It kept the same 200,000 token context window, image input support, and $15/$75 per million token pricing as Opus 4, and it gained the ability to use up to 64,000 tokens of extended thinking for harder problems. Anthropic described it as a drop-in replacement for Opus 4, meant to hold the top of the Opus line until the next full model generation shipped.

item.title: Claude Opus 4.8
item.description: Claude Opus 4.8 is Anthropic’s most capable Opus-tier model, released on May 28, 2026 as an update to Opus 4.7 that fixed some of that model’s comment-verbosity and tool-calling quirks. It scores about 88.6 percent on SWE-bench Verified and 69.2 percent on the harder SWE-bench Pro, ahead of GPT-5.5 and Gemini 3.1 Pro on the same test at the time of release, and Anthropic reports it is more likely to flag its own uncertainty rather than state unsupported claims with confidence. It supports a 1 million token input context window with up to 128,000 tokens of output, and it introduced Dynamic Workflows, a research-preview feature in Claude Code that lets the model plan a large task and then run hundreds of parallel subagents in a single session. Pricing held steady from the previous version at $5 per million input tokens and $25 per million output tokens, with a faster “fast mode” available at $10/$50.

item.title: Claude Sonnet 4
item.description: Claude Sonnet 4 launched on May 22, 2025 alongside the larger Claude Opus 4, taking the mid-tier spot in Anthropic’s Claude 4 generation. It is a hybrid reasoning model, meaning it can answer directly or work through a problem step by step in an extended thinking mode depending on the task, and Anthropic reported it hitting roughly 72.7 percent on SWE-bench Verified at launch, edging out even Opus 4 on that particular benchmark while costing a fraction of the price. It ships with a 200,000 token context window as standard, with a 1 million token context window available in beta on the API and Amazon Bedrock, and it reads images alongside text. At $3 per million input tokens and $15 per million output tokens, it became Anthropic’s default recommendation for coding and everyday agentic work where Opus-level cost isn’t justified.

item.title: Claude Sonnet 4.5
item.description: Claude Sonnet 4.5, released on September 29, 2025, was Anthropic’s highest-scoring Sonnet-tier model on SWE-bench Verified at launch, reaching about 77.2 percent on the full 500-problem set with extended thinking enabled. Anthropic built it heavily around coding and computer use, and testers reported it staying focused on a single complex task for more than 30 hours without losing track of what it was doing. It added context awareness, meaning the model tracks how much of its context window remains during a long conversation and adjusts its behavior as it fills up, which matters for agents running long unattended sessions. It kept Sonnet’s $3/$15 per million token pricing and 200,000 token standard context window, with a 1 million token context window available in beta, making it Anthropic’s primary recommendation for coding agents and long-running automation through the rest of 2025.

item.title: DeepSeek R1
item.description: DeepSeek R1 is a reasoning model released by the Chinese lab DeepSeek on January 20, 2025. It uses a 671-billion-parameter mixture-of-experts architecture with 37 billion parameters active per token, and it was trained in part with large-scale reinforcement learning rather than relying only on supervised fine-tuning, which pushed it to work through problems step by step before answering. On launch, it matched OpenAI’s o1 on math, coding, and science benchmarks (scoring 90.8 on MMLU and performing near the top of contemporary models on AIME and Codeforces-style problems) while being released with open weights under the MIT license and API pricing far below o1’s.

item.title: DeepSeek V4-Pro
item.description: DeepSeek V4-Pro is DeepSeek’s flagship model, released on April 24, 2026 alongside a smaller sibling, V4-Flash. It’s a mixture-of-experts model with 1.6 trillion total parameters and 49 billion active per token, and it introduces a hybrid attention design combining Compressed Sparse Attention and Heavily Compressed Attention that cuts inference compute and KV-cache size sharply compared to V3.2, letting it handle a 1-million-token context window. The model runs in both a “thinking” mode for step-by-step reasoning and a non-thinking mode for fast responses, and DeepSeek reports it leading open-weight models on math, science, and agentic coding benchmarks, with a SWE-bench Verified score above 80%.

item.title: DeepSeek-Math
item.description: DeepSeekMath is a 7-billion-parameter model DeepSeek built specifically for mathematical reasoning, released in February 2024 and initialized from DeepSeek-Coder-Base. It was trained on 120 billion math-related tokens pulled from web data, alongside natural language and code, and scored 51.7% on the competition-level MATH benchmark without relying on external calculators or tools, a result that at the time approached the performance of much larger closed models like Gemini-Ultra and GPT-4. DeepSeek released it in base, instruction-tuned, and reinforcement-learning-tuned variants, with the RL version trained using Group Relative Policy Optimization, an algorithm the company introduced in this paper and later reused for DeepSeek-R1. The model has a 4,096-token context window and is aimed at researchers and developers working on math tutoring, theorem proving, and quantitative reasoning tasks rather than general-purpose chat.

item.title: DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Llama-70B
item.description: DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Llama-70B is a distilled reasoning model DeepSeek released alongside DeepSeek-R1 in January 2025. Rather than training a reasoning model from scratch, DeepSeek fine-tuned Meta’s Llama 3.3 70B Instruct on reasoning traces generated by the full R1 model, transferring much of R1’s chain-of-thought problem-solving ability into a smaller, cheaper-to-run architecture. It is the largest of six distilled R1 variants DeepSeek published, spanning Qwen and Llama base models from 1.5B up to 70B parameters, and on release it scored 70.0% pass@1 on AIME 2024 and 94.5% on MATH-500, far ahead of general-purpose models like GPT-4o and Claude 3.5 Sonnet on the same math benchmarks. It carries a 128,000-token context window, inherited from its Llama 3.3 base, and is distributed under the Llama 3.3 Community License, with weights on Hugging Face and hosted API access through providers including Together AI.

item.title: DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-32B
item.description: DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-32B is a dense 32-billion-parameter model that DeepSeek built by fine-tuning Qwen2.5-32B on reasoning traces generated by the full DeepSeek-R1 model. Rather than training a smaller model from scratch, DeepSeek distilled R1’s chain-of-thought outputs into several base models, and the 32B Qwen version turned out to be the strongest of the group. It beat OpenAI’s o1-mini on math, coding, and science benchmarks despite its comparatively modest size, which made it one of the first open models small enough to run on a single high-end GPU while still showing real reasoning ability. The weights are released under the MIT license alongside the rest of the R1 family, and the model is widely mirrored on Hugging Face and served by inference providers such as Together AI and Groq.

item.title: Doubao-Seed 1.6
item.description: Doubao-Seed 1.6 is ByteDance’s reasoning-tuned model tier, announced on June 11, 2025 at Volcano Engine’s “Force” conference alongside two variants, Doubao-Seed-1.6-thinking and the lighter Doubao-Seed-1.6-flash. It supports a 256K context window and native multimodal understanding of text, images, and video within a single model, along with a configurable thinking mode that lets developers trade off latency against reasoning depth. ByteDance reported strong results on complex reasoning and competition-level math benchmarks compared to the earlier Doubao 1.5 generation.

item.title: Gemini 2.0 Flash Thinking
item.description: Gemini 2.0 Flash Thinking is an experimental reasoning variant of Gemini 2.0 Flash that Google released on December 19, 2024, shortly after the base 2.0 Flash preview. Unlike a standard chat model, it generates and shows an intermediate chain of thought before giving its final answer, similar in spirit to OpenAI’s o1, which lets users see the steps the model worked through on math, logic, and coding problems. It kept the million-token context window and multimodal input of the base Flash model.

item.title: Gemini 2.5 Pro
item.description: Gemini 2.5 Pro is Google’s reasoning-focused flagship from the 2.5 generation, released as a preview on March 25, 2025 and reaching general availability that June. It’s a “thinking” model by default, meaning it works through problems step by step internally before producing a final answer, and it handles text, image, audio, and video across a million-token context window. At launch, Google positioned it as its strongest model yet for math, science, and coding tasks, and it topped several public leaderboards including LMArena.

item.title: GPT-5
item.description: GPT-5 is the model OpenAI released on August 7, 2025, folding its previous split between fast chat models (GPT-4o) and slow reasoning models (the o-series) into one system that decides on its own how much internal reasoning a given prompt needs. Rather than making users pick a model, ChatGPT and the API route each request to a lighter or heavier internal mode automatically, cutting the number of consumer-facing choices while still letting API customers set an explicit reasoning effort. It ships with a 400K token context window (272K input, 128K output), API pricing of $1.25 per million input tokens and $10 per million output tokens, and scored around 90 on MMLU alongside strong marks on coding and agentic benchmarks at launch. OpenAI framed it as a jump in reliability and reduced hallucination rate rather than a dramatic leap in raw capability, positioning it against Google’s Gemini 2.5 Pro and Anthropic’s Claude models of the same era. By mid-2026 OpenAI had already iterated past it with the GPT-5.x line, including the GPT-5.6 family, but GPT-5 remains available in the API and ChatGPT.

item.title: GPT-5.6 Luna
item.description: GPT-5.6 Luna is the fast, low-cost tier of OpenAI’s GPT-5.6 family, which began a limited government-vetted preview in late June 2026 before opening to the wider public on July 9, 2026 once the US Commerce Department’s Center for AI Standards and Innovation cleared broader access. Luna is built for summarization, drafting, and high-volume automation where speed and cost matter more than maximum reasoning depth, and it shares the family’s 1.05 million token context window with support for up to 128,000 output tokens. At $1 per million input tokens and $6 per million output tokens, it undercuts the mid-tier Terra model by a wide margin while still handling everyday chat and lightweight coding tasks. OpenAI pitched the three-tier Sol, Terra, Luna structure as a way for developers to trade off cost against capability without switching model families, following the same pattern it used with the GPT-5 mini and nano tiers.

item.title: GPT-5.6 Sol
item.description: GPT-5.6 Sol is OpenAI’s flagship model in the GPT-5.6 family, built for frontier reasoning, complex coding, multi-step agentic work, and cybersecurity research. OpenAI first shipped it as a locked-down preview to a small group of US-government-vetted organizations in late June 2026, then opened it to the public on July 9, 2026 after regulatory review cleared wider access. It carries the family’s 1.05 million token context window and 128,000 token output limit, priced at $5 per million input tokens and $30 per million output tokens, the highest tier of the three. OpenAI says Sol launched with its most extensive safety stack yet, adding tighter controls around sensitive cyber-related requests and repeated misuse attempts given its stronger offensive and defensive security capabilities. Rather than reporting the older MMLU-style academic scores, OpenAI emphasized agentic and practical benchmarks for this release, a shift several independent reviewers noted as a departure from prior GPT-5.x announcements.

item.title: GPT-5.6 Terra
item.description: GPT-5.6 Terra is the balanced, middle tier of OpenAI’s GPT-5.6 family, aimed at everyday coding, reasoning, and agentic tasks where Sol’s top-end capability would be overkill. It reached the public on July 9, 2026, following a preview period restricted to organizations vetted by the US government, and shares the family’s 1.05 million token context window and 128,000 token output cap. OpenAI prices it at $2.50 per million input tokens and $15 per million output tokens, roughly half the cost of Sol, and describes its performance as competitive with the prior GPT-5.5 generation at that lower price. Terra is meant to be the default choice for developers who need strong reasoning and coding ability without paying flagship rates, similar to the role GPT-5’s mini tier played in the previous generation. It is available through ChatGPT, Azure OpenAI, and the standard API, and GitHub added it to Copilot the same day it launched.

item.title: GPT-OSS-120B
item.description: GPT-OSS-120B is an open-weight reasoning model OpenAI released on August 5, 2025, marking its first open model release since GPT-2 in 2019. It uses a mixture-of-experts transformer architecture with 117 billion total parameters but only about 5.1 billion active per token, which lets it run reasoning-heavy workloads on a single high-end GPU instead of the multi-GPU clusters dense models of similar size would need. It scored around 90 on MMLU at launch, putting it in the same range as OpenAI’s own o4-mini on many reasoning and coding benchmarks, and it ships under the Apache 2.0 license so companies can self-host it, fine-tune it, and run it without usage restrictions. OpenAI built it specifically to compete with open releases from Meta, Mistral, and Chinese labs like DeepSeek and Alibaba’s Qwen team, which had been setting the pace in open-weight models while OpenAI stayed closed. It is available through Hugging Face, Together AI, Azure AI Foundry, and OpenAI’s own API for organizations that want the option of both open self-hosting and managed hosting.

item.title: GPT-OSS-20B
item.description: GPT-OSS-20B is the smaller of the two open-weight models OpenAI released on August 5, 2025, alongside the larger GPT-OSS-120B, in its first open model release since GPT-2. It uses a mixture-of-experts design with about 21 billion total parameters and roughly 3.6 billion active per token, light enough to run on a single consumer GPU with 16GB or more of memory, which was the point: OpenAI built it for developers and hobbyists who wanted a capable reasoning model without server-grade hardware. It scored 85.3 on MMLU at launch, a strong result for its size class, and handles coding, math, and general reasoning tasks reasonably close to its bigger sibling despite the much smaller footprint. Released under the Apache 2.0 license, it can be fine-tuned and redistributed freely, and it is available through Hugging Face, Together AI, and OpenAI’s API for teams that want a managed option instead of self-hosting.

item.title: Grok 4
item.description: Grok 4 is xAI’s flagship model released on July 9, 2025, positioned as a reasoning-first successor to Grok 3 with heavier test-time compute and a redesigned training pipeline. At launch, Artificial Analysis measured it at the top of its Intelligence Index, ahead of OpenAI’s o3 and Google’s Gemini 2.5 Pro at the time, and xAI reported an all-time-high GPQA Diamond score near 88 percent along with a joint-best AIME 2024 score around 94 percent. It supports a 256,000-token context window and handles both text and images, and xAI made it available through the Grok app, X, and the API at $3 per million input tokens and $15 per million output tokens. Grok 4’s launch drew attention beyond benchmarks too, including scrutiny over some of its unfiltered responses on X, which xAI addressed with follow-up moderation changes. It set the baseline that xAI’s later Grok 4 Fast and Grok 4.5 releases built on through 2025 and 2026.

item.title: Grok 4.5
item.description: Grok 4.5 is xAI’s model released on July 8, 2026, built with a heavier emphasis on coding, agentic workflows, and knowledge work than earlier Grok releases. On the independent Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index it scored 54, placing fourth overall among frontier models while taking the top spot specifically on agentic tool use, and it posted 83.3 percent on Terminal-Bench 2.1 and 64.7 percent on SWE-Bench Pro, both benchmarks aimed at real coding and terminal tasks rather than multiple-choice knowledge tests. It carries a 1-million-token context window and handles text and image input, and xAI priced it at $2 per million input tokens and $6 per million output tokens, with a cheaper $0.50 rate for cached input tokens. It’s reachable through the xAI API console, the Grok app, X, and a wide set of third-party integrations including Cursor, OpenRouter, Vercel, and Microsoft’s Word, Excel, and PowerPoint add-ins. Some coverage framed it as xAI’s answer to Anthropic’s Opus-class models, given the shared focus on long agentic coding sessions.

item.title: Grok-1.5
item.description: Grok-1.5 is xAI’s follow-up to Grok-1, announced on March 29, 2024 as a step toward better reasoning and much longer context handling. Where Grok-1 topped out at 8,192 tokens, Grok-1.5 extended the context window to 128,000 tokens, letting it work through long documents and codebases in a single pass, and xAI reported gains on coding and math benchmarks compared to its predecessor. xAI did not disclose the parameter count or full architecture details for Grok-1.5, and the model was rolled out gradually to X users rather than through a public API. It served mainly as a bridge release: within months xAI had folded its improvements into Grok-2, and Grok-1.5 itself was never open-weighted the way Grok-1 was.

item.title: Hunyuan-A13B
item.description: Hunyuan-A13B is Tencent’s open-weight mixture-of-experts language model, released in June 2025 with 80 billion total parameters but only 13 billion active per token, which keeps inference cost close to a much smaller dense model. It natively supports a 256K context window, though many self-hosted setups cap it lower to fit GPU memory. The model offers a dual-mode design that lets users toggle between a fast response mode and a slower step-by-step reasoning mode for harder math, science, and coding problems. Tencent released the weights on Hugging Face under its own Hunyuan license, and the model is also available through Tencent Cloud’s API for teams that don’t want to run it themselves. It positions itself against other efficient open MoE reasoning models like DeepSeek’s smaller releases and Alibaba’s Qwen, competing more on active-parameter efficiency than raw parameter count.

item.title: InternLM2.5
item.description: InternLM2.5 is Shanghai AI Laboratory’s follow-up to InternLM2, released starting July 3, 2024 in 7B and 1.8B sizes, with a 20B version added on August 1, 2024. The 7B chat model scores 72.8 on MMLU and beats Llama 3 8B Instruct and Gemma 2 9B on several reasoning and math benchmarks, according to the developer’s own OpenCompass evaluations. A dedicated 7B-Chat-1M checkpoint extends the context window to one million tokens and can locate specific facts inside million-token documents in needle-in-a-haystack tests, while the standard 20B model tops out at 200K tokens. The series also adds stronger function calling and agent-style tool use compared to the original InternLM2, and all weights are released under the Apache 2.0 license through Hugging Face and the InternLM GitHub repository.

item.title: Kimi K1.5
item.description: Kimi K1.5 is Moonshot AI’s first reasoning-focused model, released in January 2025 as the company’s answer to OpenAI’s o1. It is trained with reinforcement learning on long chains of thought and can reason jointly over text and images, which let Moonshot claim results on par with o1 on math, coding, and multimodal benchmarks like MathVista, AIME, and Codeforces. The model supports a 128,000-token context window and includes a “long2short” technique that transfers reasoning gains from long chains of thought into shorter, faster responses for everyday queries. Moonshot has not disclosed the parameter count. K1.5 was Moonshot’s proof that a Chinese lab could compete at the reasoning frontier, and it set the stage for the open-weight Kimi K2 line that followed a few months later.

item.title: Kimi K2.6
item.description: Kimi K2.6 is Moonshot AI’s open-weight flagship model, released in April 2026 as the successor to the original Kimi K2. It is a 1-trillion-parameter mixture-of-experts model that activates about 32 billion parameters per token, ships natively in INT4 for cheaper inference, and handles a 262,144-token context window. The model is built for long-running agentic work: Moonshot designed it around multi-agent orchestration, coding sessions that run for hours without human intervention, and native multimodal input rather than bolted-on vision. Independent evaluations from Artificial Analysis rank it as the strongest open-weight model available, putting it within a few points of closed frontier systems from OpenAI and Anthropic on tasks like SWE-Bench Pro and Humanity’s Last Exam, while charging a fraction of their per-token price. Moonshot releases the weights under a modified MIT license, so anyone can download and self-host the model rather than relying on Moonshot’s own API.

item.title: Llemma 7B
item.description: Llemma 7B is a math-focused language model from EleutherAI, released in October 2023 by continuing pretraining on top of Code Llama 7B rather than starting from scratch. EleutherAI trained it further on Proof-Pile-2, a 200-billion-token mix of math papers, formal proofs, and math-heavy web text, so it specializes in chain-of-thought mathematical reasoning and can call out to tools like Python or formal theorem provers when solving problems. It comes in 7B and 34B sizes, and both were among the strongest openly available math models at the time of release. Because it inherits its base weights from Code Llama, it carries the Llama 2 Community License rather than a fully permissive one, which limits some commercial uses compared to licenses like Apache 2.0.

item.title: Mathstral
item.description: Mathstral is a 7B parameter model that Mistral AI released in July 2024, built on the Mistral 7B base and tuned specifically for math and STEM reasoning. It came out of a collaboration with Project Numina, a group focused on advancing open math models, and was released alongside Codestral Mamba as one of two specialist “miniature” models that week. On the MATH benchmark it scores 56.6%, rising to nearly 69% with majority voting across multiple samples, and it reaches 63.5% on MMLU, putting it ahead of most other models in the 7B class on quantitative reasoning tasks.
